Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Clinical Question In college-aged students (P), how does screening for depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) (I) compared to current practice (C) affect early identification of depression (O)?

Available Knowledge/Review of the Literature According to the U.S. Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF), depression is among the leading causes of disability in individuals 15 years of age and older (Siu & U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), 2016). By 2020, depressive disorders are predicted to be the second leading cause of disability and death (Soltani, Smith, Beck, & Johnson, 2014). Prevalence of depression among college students accounts for approximately 16.7% and is more than twice as common among college students compared to the general population (Liu et al., 2019; English & Campbell, 2019). Thus, depression is highly prevalent and appears to be increasing. Depression is one of the leading health concerns in college population, yet roughly half of college students with depression receive treatment (English & Campbell, 2019). Mental health among college students affects important outcomes such as social connectedness, academic performance, academic retention, and future economic productivity, which should be a significant concern for certain stakeholders such as campus administrators, college professors, and parents (Lipson, Gaddis, Heinze, & Eisenberg, 2015; Ebert et al., 2018). In addition, depression has been associated with increased health care costs such as emergency department visits and inpatient hospitalizations (Wright et al., 2015). hits.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015).
